article_text:
Picasso-Kirchner exhibition provides yet another key for understanding the multiple journeys, detours and caesuras in the evolution of several centuries of European art. Within this grand evolutionary trajectory, it becomes more fulfilling to appreciate why Picasso eventually became Picasso and Kirchner would become the artist he became.

Picasso and Kirchner in Münster

Situated in the middle of the city of Münster, Germany, the magnificent and imposing LWL-Museum fur Kunst und Kultur proudly houses 1000 years of art spanning the Middle Ages to the present times.

With such an extensive and diverse collection of artistic treasures, it is rather tempting to digest the ongoing Picasso-Kirchner exhibition at the LWL-Museum against this impressive backdrop of numerous strands of European culture and history in order to understand the antecedents, work and impact of two indisputable masters of 20 th century art.

Münster is a beguiling city with a bustling center populated by restaurants, malls, shops and bakeries. The University of Münster is located in the vicinity and is accessible by foot or cycling. There are cyclists everywhere riding at considerable speed through a landscape dotted with parks, gardens and leafy trees. There are also historic monuments amid the trees and parks attesting to a city that has seemingly blossomed amid an intriguing swathe of politics, culture and art.

Interestingly, during the epoch of absolutism, the main religio-political figure was the prince-bishop who wielded secular and religious authority in the same breath. The nobility did all they could to exert their influence and some of the art produced in this era sought to capture and project this enormous sense of power and prestige. The nobility, in turn, emphasized the continuity of lineage and secular power as symbolized by the all-pervasive coat of arms, heirlooms, aristocratic adornments and other similar emblems of authority, prestige and longevity.

Specific professions entrenched the influence of the noble class notably, the military, the clergy, civic administration and land ownership. Indeed, the preoccupations of the Westphalian artisans and artists evolved alongside the growing prestige and influence of the nobility. Accordingly, artisans competed amongst themselves to create exquisite objets d’art made of cut glass, porcelain and silver casting to the decorate the elaborate dining halls of members of the highest echelons of society.

The wider society, in turn, adopted the aesthetic proclivities the nobility suggested to it. Admirably, the palace of Münster constructed in the 18 th century by Johann Conrad Schlaun, a Baroque architect, infused Gallic influences with classical Westphalian styles.

The middle classes were not spared these Gallic influences as they aspired to embrace the promises of the French Revolution- liberty, equality and fraternity. However, the middle classes experienced considerable push back from the upper classes and had to retreat to the comfort of their homes for existential succor, ornamental refinement, cultural sophistication, and creative fulfilment.

.

Consequently, the LWL-Museum is more than merely a veritable treasure trove of the larger cultural and artistic developments in Germany alone. Indeed, it embodies the deeper wellsprings of the European cultural spirit that make it possible to appreciate the current Picasso-Kirchner exhibition from different and more varied- both optic and socio-cultural- perspectives.

During the early stages of the 20 th century, Paris, the mercurial City of Lights, drew hordes of German artists. Paula Modersohn-Becker reportedly set foot on the famed city four times between 1900 and 1906. Max Pechstein endured the winter of 1907/08 in the same metropolis.

Ernest Ludwig Kirchner and Pablo Picasso were born a year apart. And both artists were immensely influenced French avant-garde art. Although Kirchner never visited Paris unlike Picasso who spent most of his life there, he was immensely inspired by the numerous creative trends, ruptures and innovations provided by modern French art. Kirchner was particularly impressed with the works of Paul Gauguin and Henri Matisse. He would eventually pass on in 1938 (Picasso died in 1973) but fortunately, was able to produce a powerful body of work.

Indeed, at the late 2025 exhibition, there is, arguably, a more impressive showing of his work than Picasso’s. Instructively, both artists never crossed paths personally and worked independently of each other. Nonetheless, as this exhibition demonstrates, there are more than a few parallels in their separate bodies of work.

Initially, when Picasso had moved from Spain to Paris in 1904, he lived modestly, trawling the underbelly and bohemian circles of the city and comingling with beggars and other social outcasts who provided much fuel for his feverish imagination.

Kirchner, on the other hand, had re-located to Berlin in 1911 where he promptly embarked on the most productive phase of his artistic life. He found Berlin’s colorful night-life, jazz cafes and dance bars quite exhilarating and creatively liberating. These fervid and informal urban encounters emboldened his remarkable creative vision. Arguably, there were several similarities between Paris and Berlin in the early 20 th century.

In 1932, Kirchner attended a major Picasso exhibition at the Kunsthaus Zurich which led him to employ some of the latter’s formal artistic innovations and experiments in form and style.

A Dresden art gallery had mounted an exhibition of Gauguin and some German artists, including Kirchner in 1910. Kirchner had also designed the exhibition poster using an image of Gauguin’s mother. The Kirchner designed feminine visage, proudly on exhibit at the LWL-Museum, bears unambiguous exotic features as he had mistakenly thought Gauguin’s mother was of Tahitian origin. His design also displays a convincing appreciation of techniques of modern marketing and advertising and the manner in which they frequently overlap with modern pop art.

In comparing the works of Kirchner and Picasso on display, the former appears to make a more compelling statement. First of all, the LWL-Museum offers a more striking collection of Kirchner’s works. In addition, his paintings are bold, visually captivating and profoundly expressive. Picasso’s paintings, on the other hand, are uncharacteristically muted, or arguably guarded, in comparison. And as noted earlier, the themes and subject-matters of both artists are often similar when they do not directly overlap. Perhaps in somewhat minimizing Picasso’s largely often unquestioned brilliance and intimidating accomplishment, there is evident value and conceptual acuity in allowing a slightly less widely celebrated artist to breathe and gain well deserved prominence. This also speaks to a certain conceptual maneuverability and generosity on the part of the curators.

Jointly, both artists present a lavish panorama of early 20 th century European art and urban lifestyles. But even more broadly, a deeper and more lasting impression is made if the Picasso-Kirchner exhibition is savored against the rich backdrop of the European artistic heritage housed at the LWL-Museum. Through this kind of conscious juxtaposition, the continuities and ruptures across the wider currents of European art spanning several centuries would be better appreciated. And indeed, the milestones attained in European art mirrored and were often entangled in the surrounding socio-political movements and upheavals that galvanized the entire continent.

My visit to the LWL-Museum enabled a splendid discovery of what are-for me- new names of European art and also a re-affirmation of the artistic worth of old icons. August Macke who was killed in 1914 created portraits, landscapes and still life’s in the expressionist mode that reflected his personal circumstances.

Ida Gerhardi, Melchior Lechter and Bernhard Pankok collectively re-imagined the natural world in a brilliantly visual way while at the same time embodying a Parisian sensibility regarding the illumined swirl of dazzling urbanscapes.

Also accommodated in the LWL-Museum are art works by the radical German artist Joseph (1921-1986). Beuys sought to democratize the art making process by making small-scale multiples in easy-to-handle forms, shapes and sizes and at affordable prices. Hans Arp and Max Ernst are also well represented attesting to their fifty-year-old relationship and creative development as major artists.

Such is the range and diversity of artists, traditions and centuries to be found within the remarkable interiors of the LWL-Museum.

Against this visually stunning background, the Picasso-Kirchner exhibition provides yet another key for understanding the multiple journeys, detours and caesuras in the evolution of several centuries of European art. Within this grand evolutionary trajectory, it becomes more fulfilling to appreciate why Picasso eventually became Picasso and Kirchner would become the artist he became. Some of the more obvious splendors of this exhibition, as such, not only lie in the productive staged conversations between Picasso and Kirchner, but even more broadly speaking, between their numerous peers and also their esteemed forebears who did so much to pave the way for great 20 th century art.

LWL-Museum für Kunst und Kultur, Münster Until 18.1.2026

Kirchner Museum Davos 15.2. – 3.5.2026

editorial_title_zh: 《Blue Film》：这部备受争议的色情网络主播剧情片是如何仅用100,000美元制作出来的

article_text:
The cast and crew of “ Blue Film ” were popping the champagne when disaster struck. The microbudget drama had just wrapped its final shot, managing to complete the controversial story of a cam boy and his pedophile client in 11 days and for just $45,000. That’s when Bijan Kazerooni, one of the film ‘s producers, was called over to talk to cinematographer Ryan Jackson-Healy in his car.

“He is sitting there white-knuckling the steering wheel, and he goes, ‘We lost the day,'” Kazerooni remembered.

The production’s hard drive had failed, meaning they lost all the footage they had shot that day, including a wrenching monologue performed by Reed Birney, the film’s star. After taking a breath, Kazerooni cobbled together an additional day of photography.

“We had to call everybody back for that 12th day, and because it’s last minute, not all of our crew was available, so we had to find new people, and we had to extend the actors’ hotels for a day, and change the flights,” Kazerooni said. “That’s the thing that really kicks your ass on these tiny budgets, because I can negotiate with a camera shop about pricing all day long. I can’t negotiate with Delta Airlines.”

In the end, the filmmakers shot “Blue Film” for $50,000 and spent an additional $50,000 on post-production. Much of the money came from indie maverick Mark Duplass, who challenged the producers and writer/director Elliott Tuttle to make a film on a shoestring budget.

“You can’t do half a day on production on a union shoot for $50,000,” Kazerooni said. “You can’t make a short film for $50,000 anymore. I’ve produced short films since ‘Blue Film’ that have cost more than our entire production budget.”

“Blue Film” hit that target because Tuttle purposely designed the movie to be as cost-efficient as possible. There are just two characters: Birney, who plays a john with a dark secret, and Kieron Moore, who stars as a fetish camboy who agrees to spend the night. Most of the film, meanwhile, was shot in one location: a Hancock Park house owned by the friend of producer Waylon Sall. It cost the production $1,000 to rent for the month.

“They had just moved out of their home, and the new tenant hadn’t moved in yet, so I was able to get a favorable deal,” Sall said. “We shot there for pennies and were able to dress it like a vacant Hollywood Airbnb.”

The actors worked for scale, which also kept costs to a minimum. But the production made a point of putting backend participation into contracts. Of course, assembling the cast had its challenges. Birney, a Tony Award winner with memorable turns on screen in “Mass” and “The Menu,” knew Adam Kersh, one of the producers. But finding the right actor to play Aaron Eagle, the sex worker who captivates Birney’s character, took some maneuvering.

“It was harder to attach a casting director because of the content of the movie than it was to attach Reed,” Kersh said. “We had a lot of passes. They were all afraid of it.”

Fortunately, Eleonore Hendricks, whose credits include “Stand Clear of the Closing Doors,” signed on, which helped legitimize the production. She discovered Moore, an English actor who appeared in “Boots” and “Vampire Academy.”

“Blue Film” also benefited from other experienced hands, including Jackson-Healy, who served as cinematographer on “Mass,” and editor Zach Clark (“Our Son”). It also relied on several volunteer PAs.

“My housemates would come with me at two a.m. to load out and load in,” admits Kazerooni.

Though Birney and Moore were used to more creature comforts, they embraced the micro-budget atmosphere.

“Both of our talent are nonlocal, so flying them out and putting them up for a little over 20 days, from a budget standpoint, was awful,” Kazerooni said. “But they were very patient with me when I called them and proposed certain flights that were maybe not the class they would have wanted. What made everything possible was a willingness from our cast and from our crew to tolerate indie film conditions and to not balk at things.”

And the actors were willing to suffer for their art. Moore, for instance, spends the second half of the film shirtless after allowing Birney’s character to shave his chest.

“We had to shoot everything with him with hair, then get the hair off,” Sall said. “Kieron didn’t want to be shaved. He wanted to get waxed. So, we have one night before a two-day break. We finish shooting and call a waxing place to stay open late for us, so we can take Kieron straight from set to the salon. Kieron had a lot of hair. He’s British. He’s pale. He was in a lot of pain. He pushed himself to the limit. I was there with him. He was screaming that he wanted to kill me, but you know the results are undeniable. It gave him a natural, razor-burn look. I wish there were a less painful alternative, but it worked.”

Kersh is a veteran manager and publicist who produced the indie hit “Between the Temples,” but the rest of the production team was relatively new to features.

“We were all figuring out how to make a tiny, tiny movie together,” said Will Youmans, one of the producers. “But it was great to find a group of people who wanted to do something together and who just decided to make it happen.”

Tuttle acknowledges the film was a no-frills affair, but credits the producers with letting him focus on putting the story on screen without getting consumed by the cost of everything.

“I was never worried about anything production-wise — not once,” Tuttle said. “It seems insane to think about making a movie for that number in that amount of days. But because of my team, I didn’t have to think about the logistical nightmare of making an indie film. I just got to be creatively fulfilled.”

However, even after the film came in on budget, finding a distributor for the hot-button project wasn’t easy. Sundance, SXSW, and other major festivals all passed after screening the movie. Finally, the Edinburgh Festival stepped up and accepted the film. That’s when critics embraced the picture , raising its profile.

“Premiering in Scotland changed everything,” Kersh said.

Eventually, Obscured Releasing , a newcomer to the distribution scene, bought the film’s U.S. rights and released it in theaters last summer. It earned $144,371 in limited release and found a wider audience when it premiered on demand. Kersh says the film is poised to recoup its initial investment and distribution expenses. It is expected to turn a profit. “Blue Film” has also secured distribution in international markets, including the U.K., Germany, and Latin America. Despite some setbacks, the producers believe that “Blue Film” is more successful than a movie about a camboy and a pedophile could have ever hoped to be.

“I get lots of calls from people being like, ‘How do I get money for my film? How do I pull off something like this?'” said Youmans. “And the answer is like, you get money for your movie the way you get money for anything in your life, which is any way you can. There’s no magic to it.”
excerpt_original: The story of a sex worker and his john was too hot for major film festivals, but thanks to its microbudget, it's a box-office success.

article_text:
Films and events

Create

Easter

Sekja, an ageing and charismatic Korean trans burlesque star, is front and centre in this glorious film about life.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Mokya Shin

With Saekja, Jinhyo Lim, Rosemary

South Korea 2026. 84min

Courtesy of Low Light Films

Language Korean With English subtitles

Introduction

As the spotlight fades and ornate costumes are put away, Sekja, an elder in the Korean adult entertainment scene, reflects on her life. We are made privy to her thoughts on love, connection and being honest narrators of our own story. Intriguing dance sequences and astonishingly lush aesthetics bring Sekja’s story to life, making Easter a often touching feast of thought and image.

Lynn Nwokorie

Content advice

Contains scenes of nudity.

Contains transphobic attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Sweet Milk Lake

In writer-director-actor Harvey Zielinski’s coming-of-age drama, a young trans man’s homecoming results in unexpected consequences when he’s mistaken for his cisgender twin brother.

Elephants in the Fog

A parent’s search for their missing child disrupts the fragile coexistence between Nepal’s kinnar community and the rest of a village’s population.

I Plant My Hand in the Garden

Playing versions of themselves as the central protagonists, Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija make a daring debut: a witty, irreverent and politically astute portrait of lives shaped by the search for belonging.

article_text:
“6TM,” directed by Karim Akalay and produced by Walid Bekhti, won the New Visions Award for the most promising European project at the Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival on Friday. The film is described as “a Belgian family comedy in three chapters, rooted in magic realism and the resilience of a community.”

In the film, which is set over one scorching summer in the Cité Modèle, Brussels’ largest housing project, three stories unfold across one family. Two kids chase a magic lamp to keep their wheelchair-using friend from being forced out by broken elevators. A teenage girl builds a team of misfits for a soccer tournament. A mother rallies her neighbors to uncover who stole the rain.

Related Stories

Ethan Klein Reacts to Hila Klein's Cheating Allegations Amid 'H3 Podcast' Fallout: 'Please Respect My Family's Privacy ... They Have Nothing to Do With This'

The jury said, “With its imaginative blend of magical realism, humor and social relevance, ‘6TM ‘ offers a fresh vision of European cinema. Rooted in lived experience and shaped through co-creation, ‘6TM’ challenges conventional representations and opens up new possibilities for who gets to tell stories, whose voices are heard, and who sees themselves reflected on screen. We believe this approach holds extraordinary promise for the next generation of both audiences and filmmakers, demonstrating how cinema can become more inclusive and participatory.”

The jury was composed of Katrine Kiilgaard, managing director of CPH:DOX in Denmark; Anda Ionescu, managing partner and producer at Tangaj Production in Romania; and Robert Y. Chang, co-producer of American Documentary at POV in the U.S.

The award was presented in cooperation with UPP, which donated an in-kind grant for visual post-production worth about 15,000 Euros, and Soundaquare, which provided sound mixing and a final sound master, with an estimated value of 5,000 Euros.

The New Visions Award for the most promising U.S. project went to “Searching for SmarterChild,” directed by Lindsey Sitz and Zan Gillies, and produced by Erin Williams-Weir.

The U.S.-Canadian film looks back to 2003, and the creation of SmarterChild, an online chatbot. He became a sounding board for a generation. People confided in him, insulted him and propositioned him.

Twenty years later, as AI becomes deeply embedded in our lives, what does our treatment of the first internet chatbot say about us? By revisiting our cringe-worthy conversations, the film explores the darkest parts of human nature, accountability, and what it takes to change, not only the technologies we create, but ourselves.

The jury said, ” ‘Searching for SmarterChild’ takes us back to the early days of the internet to confront one of the most pressing questions of our time: what does our relationship with artificial intelligence reveal about ourselves? By revisiting their interactions with one of the earliest chatbots of their childhoods, the filmmakers offer a perspective on today’s fascination with AI, challenging us to reflect not only on the technologies we create, but also on how we treat them and each other. The jury wishes to recognize the project’s promise to engage audiences through an original, entertaining and thought-provoking approach to a subject that will profoundly shape our collective future.”

The award was presented in partnership with AmDocs, with the winner receiving $7,000 in cash.

The festival also accorded the APA World Excellence Award to renowned Danish producer Signe Byrge Sørensen. The award honors her “outstanding contribution to international film production and her remarkable achievements in world cinema.”

article_text:
On the night of Feb. 3, 1972, the prints of “ Pakeezah ” arrived at Bombay’s Maratha Mandir cinema in a palanquin pulled by four horses. Military bands played outside, police held back the thousands crowding the gates, and inside, the film’s star, Meena Kumari , sat beside her husband, director Kamal Amrohi, and gripped his wrist so hard through the screening that her nails drew blood.

Amrohi’s son Tajdar was in the theater that night. His father never pulled his arm away.

“He just gave a smile, and she also smiled in an embarrassment, you can say,” Tajdar Amrohi says. “And it seems that even after 54 years, I feel as if that incident took place yesterday.”

Kumari died on March 31, 1972, weeks after the film opened. Now, Film Heritage Foundation’s (FHF) 4K restoration of “Pakeezah,” carried out with the Amrohi family, is back in front of audiences. Thierry Frémaux presents its world premiere at Festival Lumière in Lyon on Wednesday. It then plays a gala at the BFI London Film Festival ’s BFI Imax on Oct. 18 that Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, the foundation’s director, will introduce with Tajdar Amrohi, his sister Rukhsar Amrohi and Kamal Amrohi’s grandson Bilal Amrohi. Dungarpur says he heard the Imax screening sold out “in no time.”

The film is set in Lucknow as the age of the nawabs (Muslim nobles) fades. Kumari plays Sahibjaan, born in a graveyard to a courtesan who was spurned by her husband’s aristocratic family. Raised in a brothel, Sahibjaan grows up to be the most celebrated courtesan of her day, though she longs for love and respectability. Then Salim, a forest officer played by Raaj Kumar, wanders into her train compartment by mistake while she is asleep. Taken with her feet, he leaves her a note in verse and slips away. When they meet again, they fall in love, but the stigma attached to her profession stands between them.

Few Indian films carry a backstory as heavy as this one. Amrohi was already married, with three children, when he married Kumari. Rukhsar grew up with her mother in the family’s hometown of Amroha, in Uttar Pradesh, until she was 13, while her father lived in Bombay (now Mumbai) with Kumari, whom the children called Chhoti Ammi (little mother). Amrohi conceived “Pakeezah” in the mid-1950s around Kumari, his wife and muse, and shooting began in 1956, in black-and-white, before moving to Eastmancolor and then CinemaScope. The production stalled in 1964 when the couple separated, and Kumari’s health declined sharply over the following years. The film’s German cinematographer, Josef Wirsching, who had come with Himansu Rai and Devika Rani from Bombay Talkies, died partway through. Composer Ghulam Mohammed died in 1968 after writing the songs, leaving Naushad to complete the background score.

Through all of it, Amrohi refused to let the film go.

“His relations, his health, his wealth – he put everything into ‘Pakeezah,’” his daughter Rukhsar Amrohi says.

She remembers that every household request, from new decor to things for himself, got the same answer: after “Pakeezah.” His kurtas (tunics), which usually arrived from Lucknow a dozen at a time every six months, wore thin during the shoot. When she pressed him to reorder, he told her that people came to see him, not his clothes.

“I’ll order all of this after ‘Pakeezah’ – not 12, I’ll get 24 – but let my ‘Pakeezah’ get into theaters,” she recalls him saying.

Tajdar Amrohi says that by the time the film was ready for release, his father didn’t have a penny to keep for himself and was deep in debt. Financiers, Rukhsar says, pushed him to drop Ghulam Mohammed’s music as old-fashioned and credit popular composers of the time Laxmikant-Pyarelal or Shankar-Jaikishan instead. He refused, whether or not that meant the film got made.

The family’s own life bent around the production. When Kumari left and the shoot stopped, Amrohi sent Rukhsar and her mother back to Amroha. He didn’t want anyone to say that his first wife and daughter had arrived and driven Kumari out. He later wrote to Rukhsar asking her to raise her small hands in prayer that he would finish the picture. He had expected to complete it in a year, and it now felt like a noose around his neck.

“Isn’t that a sacrifice?” she says.

When shooting resumed, the haveli (mansion) set on Stage 3 at Filmistan Studio in Goregaon was modeled on the Amrohis’ ancestral home in Amroha. Rukhsar went to the set every day because her father wanted her there. She also traveled with the unit to Mysore for the outdoor shoot of the song “Mausam Hai Aashiqana” and the elephant attack sequence. Her mother’s paandaan (a box for paan, or betel leaf), part of her wedding trousseau, was lent at Amrohi’s request. It appears in the Gulabi Mahal (Pink Palace) scenes beside the actor Nadira. It now sits in the drawing room of the Amroha house, which Rukhsar restored and filled with her father’s furniture, photographs and belongings. Locals, she says, began calling it Kamal Amrohi’s museum.

The siblings are protective of how their father’s marriage is remembered. Tajdar Amrohi is adamant that the couple never divorced, and says that Kumari had asked Amrohi to promise he never would, calling him Chandan, her pet name for him. He also pushes back on the widely told account that actors Sunil Dutt and Nargis and composer Khayyam persuaded Kumari to return to the film in 1969. Dutt deserves credit for going to her, he says, but many others in the industry, Ashok Kumar among them, had urged the same.

“Frankly speaking, if Meena ji herself hadn’t wanted to complete this film, she wouldn’t have,” he says.

Nor, he says, did “Pakeezah” become a hit because its star died weeks after release, a reading his sister also rejects. If that were how it worked, he argues, “Every producer-director would pray that once the film is complete, one of their main artists leaves the world, and the film will be a hit. That’s not how it is. A good thing is good, and a bad thing is bad and won’t run.”

Tajdar Amrohi was at St. Elizabeth Nursing Home on Malabar Hill when Kumari died, and says it was the first time he had ever seen tears in his father’s eyes. Amrohi died in 1993 and is buried beside her. His son sees that as a kind of divine verdict on decades of gossip about the pair.

“Just as Shah Jahan immortalized Mumtaz Mahal by building the Taj Mahal, Kamal sahab [sir] immortalized Chhoti Ammi, Meena ji, across the whole world by making ‘Pakeezah,’” he says.

For Rukhsar Amrohi, who also calls Kumari Chhoti Ammi, the film is a token of the couple’s love, made by her father out of his love for Kumari. “‘Pakeezah’ is the love child of our Baba [father] and Chhoti Ammi,” she says.

For Dungarpur, the film goes back to his own childhood. He was three when it was released, and his grandmother, Usha Rani, the Maharani (queen) of Dumraon in Bihar, was obsessed with it. She played its LP and later took him to see it on rerelease. He founded FHF in her memory in 2014 and had wanted to restore “Pakeezah” ever since.

“It’s one of my most beautiful memories of restoration, and the most important film in my life,” he says. “She was the driving force on seeing this restoration.”

The job turned out to be among the hardest the foundation has taken on. When the FHF team examined the film’s original camera negative at a Mumbai lab, it had melted, with no images left on the celluloid.

“Meena ji went into a coma two days before her death, and the negative of ‘Pakeezah’ had also gone into a coma,” Tajdar Amrohi says.

The team rebuilt the film from an interpositive, a CinemaScope print and a color reversal internegative held at the National Film Archive of India, which Dungarpur credits to archivist P.K. Nair. The sound negative had also survived. The two-year restoration was carried out at L’Immagine Ritrovata in Bologna, with the soundtrack remixed in 5.1.

The on-and-off shoot left its own scars. Day-for-night sequences didn’t match from one stretch of the film to the next. The opticals, meaning the fades and shot changes, drifted in and out of focus. Padma Khanna and other doubles performed some of the dances instead of Kumari, which made the continuity puzzle harder.

Color was the biggest test. The available versions had faded badly, and accounts differed on whether Kumari’s costume in the “Inhi Logon Ne” song was pink or red. Original color photographs were scarce, since continuity stills were usually shot in black-and-white to save money. FHF found a few, and Rukhsar Amrohi, who had been on set, came to Dungarpur’s studio to check them. She told him the lyric itself mentions a dupatta (scarf) dyed pink, so red couldn’t be right, and pushed for a deep magenta. That is what made it to the screen.

“You have to make sure that you don’t do something which he had not done, or you enhance it to that level, but keep it exactly his vision, the way he had conceived the film,” Dungarpur says.

He points viewers to the tracking shot at the end of the “Chalte Chalte” song where the camera glides over a fountain. For him it shows what the film’s camera team pulled off before zoom lenses were in common use. The film also has an anniversary this month: Dungarpur notes that Oct. 8 marked the 100th birthday of its male lead, Raaj Kumar, who replaced an aging Ashok Kumar as Salim.

FHF has run into missing negatives before. Dungarpur says the restored “Sholay” had the same problem. So did the foundation’s work on “English, August,” which was rebuilt from a single print, and Shaji N. Karun’s Cannes winner “Piravi,” for which only subtitled prints survive.

“So much money is spent on the production, so much money is spent, but there’s very little money spent on preserving these elements,” he says. “And that’s been quite a tragic story of India’s cinematic history.”

The foundation has had a busy 12 months on the festival circuit. It took “ In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones ” to Berlin, “ Amma Ariyan ” to Cannes and “ English, August ” to Venice, with stops including New York, Toronto, Shanghai, Singapore and the Festival of Three Continents. Dungarpur says FHF deliberately programs Indian commercial landmarks such as “Sholay,” “Pakeezah” and “Amar Akbar Anthony” next to independent titles. That way, Western audiences who would otherwise never see them get the chance. “Pakeezah” is set to travel to the Smithsonian and the Academy Museum, and its producers plan a wide release in India.

FHF’s next restorations are Shyam Benegal’s “Bhumika” and “Mandi,” John Abraham’s “Agraharathil Kazhuthai” (“Donkey in a Brahmin Village”) and Aribam Syam Sharma’s “Imagi Ningthem” (“My Son, My Precious”). The Abraham film will be the foundation’s first Tamil-language restoration. With Criterion, FHF is restoring Bimal Roy’s “Bandini,” “Devdas” and “Madhumati” as well as Satyajit Ray’s “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,” and it plans to take on “Piravi.”

Tajdar Amrohi still regrets that “Pakeezah” won no major awards. When he once complained about it to his father, the director just smiled.

“You haven’t noticed one thing,” he told his son. “All these people who are coming to watch the picture – that is my award.”

article_text:
絵本作家エリック・カールの回顧展、数々の名作を公開！

東京都現代美術館で7月26日まで開催された 「エリック・カール展 はじまりは、はらぺこあおむし」は、 福岡県立美術館（10月23日～12月20日）に巡回後、 2027年3月20日（土）から5月9日（日）まで、あべのハルカス美術館（大阪）で開催されます。

本展はアメリカを代表する絵本作家エリック・カール（1929～2021年）の回顧展です。ページごとに紙のサイズが変わり、あおむしの食べた跡が穴で表現されている絵本『はらぺこあおむし』は、現在でも世界中のこども達に愛されています。本展は『はらぺこあおむし』日本語版50周年を記念して、米国・マサチューセッツ州にあるエリック・カール絵本美術館とともに開催します。 ◇「エリック・カール展 はじまりは、はらぺこあおむし」福岡県立美術館で10月23日から12月20日まで

エリック・カール展 はじまりは、はらぺこあおむし Eric Carle: Art, Books, and the Caterpillar

会場：あべのハルカス美術館（大阪市阿倍野区阿倍野筋1-1-43 あべのハルカス16階）

会期：2027年3月20日（土）～5月9日（日）

開館時間：火～金 10:00～20:00、月土日祝 10:00～18:00 ※入場は閉館の30分前まで

公式サイト 公式X ： @ericcarle26_27 公式Instagram： @ericcarle26_27

＊休館日、観覧料等の情報は、確定し次第、展覧会公式サイト等でお知らせします。 ＊展示作品、会期等については、今後の諸事情により変更する場合があります。最新情報は展覧会公式サイト等でご確認ください。

『はらぺこあおむし』（1969年）や『パパ、お月さまとって！』（1986年）、『10このちいさなおもちゃのあひる』（2005年）など27冊の絵本の原画にあわせ、グラフィックデザイナー時代の作品、アイディアの最初の構想段階で作られるダミーブック、コラージュに使用する素材(色や模様をつけた紙)など、約180点を展示します。原画の色鮮やかさ、デザイナーとしての造本の工夫、そして絵本に込めたこども達への優しいまなざしを体験できます。

エリック・カール Eric Carle

1929年6月25日、アメリカ・ニューヨーク州にてドイツからの移民である両親のもとに生まれる。6歳の頃、両親と共にドイツに移住するが、ナチス政権における戦時でもあり、灰色の少年時代を送る。シュトゥットガルト州立芸術アカデミーでグラフィックデザインを学び、1952年ニューヨークに戻り、デザイナーやアートディレクターとして活躍する。 1967年、作家のビル・マーティン・Jrの絵本『くまさん くまさん なにみてるの？』にイラストレーションを描いたことから絵本作家への道が開ける。ページの開き方や形に工夫を凝らし、光や音などの仕掛けを加えた「遊べる本であり、読めるおもちゃ」を目指した点に特徴がある。2002年、マサチューセッツ州アマーストにアメリカ初の絵本専門美術館「エリック・カール絵本美術館」開館。2021年5月23日、マサチューセッツ州ノーサンプトンにて91歳で亡くなる。

article_text:
Stepping outside the airport in Mallorca, three-time Oscar-nominee cinematographer Matthew Libatique was taken aback by the light. He briefly delayed greetings so he could take it all in: the way the autumnal sun kissed baby-pink buildings and glistened against the island’s shores before setting behind the mountains.

This is an experience the veteran DP shared while speaking at Evolution Mallorca , the Spanish island’s leading film festival, where he is this year’s recipient of the Cinematography Icon Award.

When taking into consideration how passionate Libatique seems to be about the natural, how is he dealing with the fast-paced changes brought by artificial intelligence? The matter seems even more pertinent to the cinematographer, whose longest creative collaborator is “Black Swan” director Darren Aronofsky . The “Noah” filmmaker launched AI studio Primordial Soup last year in collaboration with Google DeepMind and is currently heavily invested in understanding how the technology might shape the future of cinema.

Asked by Variety whether or not he and Aronofsky have spoken about how AI might affect their collaboration, Libatique says they are currently “testing” the technology ahead of shooting their next film together. “We’ve discussed it,” he says. “We’re doing a test soon. I have a belief that the more you give to the system, the more it’s gonna have what you’re looking for. He wants to see how little you can do; we both want to learn more about it.”

The “Iron Man” cinematographer adds that AI “won’t replace cinema.” “What it could replace is Marvel,” he adds, clarifying that the major studio and others like DC “make these giant films and technology is clearly a part of it.” “They make their movies for so much money, I can understand why, through visual effects, they are going to have to employ AI to curb some of their costs,” he goes on, noting how he doesn’t think, however, that Marvel “will ever use AI actors.”

“They’ve always been able to get a personality into the characters, whether it’s Chris Evans or Robert Downey Jr.; these people become these characters people fall in love with,” he says. “I don’t think there’s going to be a Tilly Norwood Batwoman or Black Widow. You can’t tell me you’re going to make an AI character that can do what Robert Pattinson does. You can’t.”

Libatique brings up Zach Snyder’s “300” as an example of a film that could become an AI product in today’s day and age. The 2006 epic was filmed almost entirely against green screens in a massive warehouse, with the creative team constructing almost all landscapes digitally. “It was basically our early AI movie. If you want your movie to look that way, go for it. But, again, how do we connect [to it] as humans? The audience for some of these films is really limited. It’s limited by age, gender, and also by social interaction.”

“Nobody’s going to make ‘Sentimental Value’ with AI,” he emphasizes. “So I would pump the brakes on the idea that it is going to replace us all, because I don’t think there is going to be a time when we as a society turn our backs on cinema because we need it.”

Returning to Aronofsky, while Libatique can’t reveal further details on their next project and the full extent AI will be used in it, he is adamant the film will remain “human.” “We’re gonna make it like a movie. We’re gonna stand on set. Darren is gonna get on his knees, and he’s gonna move everything around with his fingers, and he’ll do what he usually does. But it’s a different thing, the AI. I don’t think it’s replacing what he does, but he’s interested.”

The cinematographer says one of the things the duo is discussing is “using the camera the way we use the camera and then see what this technology can do.” “[Aronofsky] has been given money to be able to explore this, so I applaud him for that. I feel I need to understand it better. I think you have to.”

While Libatique is “annoyed” by conversations around the technology, he can also see its benefits. The maestro DP says he has used AI in post-production and can see it being helpful to his craft when it comes to correcting glare, for example. “The machine learning how to do that is helpful to me, rather than sending it to another country so that some people who are getting $2 an hour can do it,” he adds.

When prodded as to how the technology is stripping away jobs from post-production experts, Libatique is quick to recognize the harsh reality of that situation. “I feel for them,” he says. “It’s insensitive for me to revel in the fact that I can do some of the things in a room that we can do now because it definitely took some work away. But that work was taken away from people in our industry anyway, and it was given to basically sweatshops in other countries. I guess the question is when does it end? When does it start really replacing people? It’s a mental exercise to try to figure that out: when is the next shoe that’s going to drop that’s going to affect everyone?”

The cinematographer recently had a parallel experience with AI usage in filmmaking when he shot Dustin Yellin’s “Goodbye Lamby.” The short film sees the director use artificial intelligence to imagine a world within one of his most famous sculptures. “In the old days, if you wanted to do it, you could do it with stop motion animation,” says Libatique. “But because we now have this thing that everybody is so enamored of, they made it in AI. And it was relatively successful because you’re not dealing with reality there.”

Libatique was surprised when the person responsible for the AI prompting asked him to physically light a space for a scene before she could move on with her work. “I talked to the person doing the prompting; there were things that she needed physically from me for her to create a shortcut for prompting,” he notes. “It was easier to place a light in the hole in the roof than it is for her to try to convince [the machine] to do what she wants.”

The “A Star Is Born” cinematographer is also concerned with how AI “pulls its references” and issues of creative copyright. “On two occasions, someone has sent me AI videos where the machine was told to shoot in the style of Matthew Libatique,” he recalls. “How come everything I do is out for grabs? That’s absolutely offensive. I mean, I am flattered that somebody sent me this video, but it’s horrible.”

“I don’t have a distinctive style. I always try to find a story in what I do,” he goes on. “I don’t try to impose myself on a movie. I only impose myself in the sense that I’m trying to understand who the director I’m working with is so that I can use my skills to help that vision, whether it’s Olivia Wilde or Jodie Foster or Jon Favreau. AI is all the same; it’s so plastic. To take everything I’ve done and distill it into a style that is uniquely mine is completely incorrect.”

“The other thing is: who is in charge of prompting? Who has taste? The human element is what makes all films different,” he adds. “I already have a problem with how everything kind of looks the same [today]. Lighting has become homogeneous in films. Everything is like a Temu David Fincher. I see him over and over again because he’s such a visual reference for many of us. For me, what matters is the end result, and I haven’t seen anything created by AI that’s really impressed me – and I am not sure I will.”
